Photograph: Dave Decker/ZUMA Press Wire/Shutterstock US midterm elections 2026 Democratic socialist Angie Nixon clinches surprise primary win in Florida US Senate race Nixon bested Alexander Vindman to win Democratic nomination and now faces Republican Ashley Moody in November Trump-backed Byron Donalds wins Republican primary in race to succeed Florida governor DeSantis Richard Luscombe Tue 18 Aug 2026 20.26 EDT Last modified on Tue 18 Aug 2026 20.48 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google In an upset for the Democratic establishment, progressive Angie Nixon won the party’s US Senate primary in Florida , beating former army intelligence officer Alexander Vindman. Nixon, a state representative and member of the Democratic Socialists of America, had significantly less funding going into the primary – with $975,000 to Vindman’s $16.3m at the end of July, according to Florida Politics . Vindman was previously better known for being a whistleblower leading to Trump’s first impeachment in 2019 after the US president sought to withhold military aid to Ukraine. Democrats have their sights set on upsetting Republican Ashley Moody in the US Senate general election. Moody, picked by DeSantis to replace Marco Rubio when he became secretary of state last year, won what was almost a token primary election to run in November to serve the remaining two years of Rubio’s term. https://telex.hu/kulfold/2026/10/16/ukra.text: Menü Kereső Ukrán külügyminiszter: Magyar Péter bölcs hozzáállással elérte azt, amit Orbán zsarolással soha Külföld Nyilas Gergely Állítsd be a Telexet megbízható forrásnak! Beállítom Magyar Péter és Volodimir Zelenszkij első tárgyalása után méltatta a két ország látványosan javuló kapcsolatát az ukrán külügyminiszter is, reagálva Orbán Anita nem sokkal korábbi, szintén pozitív hangvételű bejegyzésére , amelyben a magyar külügyminiszter kijelentette, hogy a két ország vezetése a teljes magyar–ukrán kapcsolatrendszer megújításán dolgozik. Andrij Szibiha válaszul kitért arra, hogy a magyar kormányfő és az ukrán elnök pénteki találkozója mellett a külügyminiszteri szintű tárgyalást is megtartották, amely hozzájárul a kapcsolatok új alapokra helyezéséhez, „gazdasági, humanitárius, politikai és egyéb téren”. „Sok területen van még tennivalónk, de már egyértelműen kimondhatjuk: ez egy új fejezet. Történelmi. Közösen bebizonyítottuk, hogy a nyugodt diplomácia kölcsönösen kifizetődő. […] Magyar Péter miniszterelnök és csapata néhány hónap alatt elérte azt bölcs, együttműködő hozzáállással, amit Orbán Viktor képtelen volt elérni éveken át tartó zsarolással” – jelentette ki Szibiha, a gazdasági, infrastrukturális, határokon átívelő együttműködés megvalósításának, az „erősebb Európa” közös építésének fontosságát kiemelve. A diplomata szintén kitért arra, hogy a kormányközi bizottságok folytatják a kétoldalú munkát „a kölcsönösen gyümölcsöző együttműködés érdekében”, mert a két ország „megérdemli a jószomszédi kapcsolatokat, és a közös jövőt a békés Európában”. https://www.politico.eu/article/some-oil.text: BRUSSELS — Some of the world's biggest oil companies will be able to promote themselves as green investments in the EU under an overhaul of the bloc's sustainable finance rules. EU member countries and lawmakers struck a deal late Thursday to update the Sustainable Finance Disclosure Regulation that will make it easier for private investment earmarked for green activities to flow into new fossil fuel projects. It was Big Oil's second big European win of the day, after the EU agreed early Thursday to delay methane emission rules for fossil fuel companies for two years. Advertisement Advertisement The sustainable finance agreement substantially loosens a proposal by the European Commission to get more money flowing into companies that are switching from dirtier to cleaner business models. The executive decided to overhaul the SFDR, which aims to prevent greenwashing and help investors make sustainable investment decisions, last November. It proposed introducing three new categories for green funds — ESG basics, Transition and Sustainable — which each have progressively stricter sustainability criteria. EU countries and the European Parliament had disagreed over whether fossil fuel companies should be allowed in the new "transition" category. The Commission proposed a blanket exclusion, but member countries pushed for oil companies with greener ambitions to be included. The Parliament, meanwhile, only wanted oil and gas companies to be allowed if they invest more in green activities than in new oil and gas projects over a three-year period. Under Thursday's final agreement, seen by POLITICO, the EU has ruled that companies will have to spend one-fifth of their capital expenditure on green activities and this will have to “meaningfully” increase “over time” and be measured annually. The increase in green investment cannot be “merely marginal or nominal,” the rules specified. The 20% capex threshold will be reviewed by the Commission in five years. Advertisement Advertisement Companies will also have to produce a Paris-aligned emissions reduction plan for some of their emissions. However, downstream emissions — which represent the biggest share of oil and gas companies’ emissions — will not have to be covered by these plans. The EU’s finance chief, Maria Luís Albuquerque, told POLITICO that the final deal was “close enough” to the Commission’s proposal as she left the meeting. The outcome could see big oil and gas companies like France’s TotalEnergies and Spain’s Repsol qualify for financing under the transition category, based on their 2025 capital expenditure. The French oil giant met with the lead Parliament negotiator, Dutch MEP Gerben-Jan Gerbrandy, three times between the start of 2025 and June 2026, according to Parliament documents . Aleksandra Palinska, executive director at sustainable finance trade association Eurosif, said the criteria agreed by the co-legislators on the transition category “fail to distinguish companies genuinely transforming their business models from those making isolated green investments.” Capitals win EU capitals proposed a more lenient approach than the Commission and Parliament, agreeing in June that Big Oil could be included in the transition category if companies spend one-fifth of their capital expenditure on green activities, as defined under the EU taxonomy on sustainable investments. Advertisement Advertisement This is despite several EU countries advocating for a move away from fossil fuels and publishing fossil fuel phase-out plans at COP31 this month. Lawmakers in October voted for big oil and gas companies to only be included in the category if they invest more in green activities than in new fossil fuel projects over a three-year period. Several EU countries — including France and Italy — saw the Parliament’s position as a “red line,” according to a document seen by POLITICO, with the final agreement landing closer to what EU capitals wanted. Despite this, Gerbrandy, who led negotiations in Parliament, said he was happy with the agreement. “I think we achieved a result that is in accordance with the criteria I set — credibility and administrative burdens — so I’m very satisfied,” he said.

https://www.dw.com/en/peter-magyar-meets.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5PtkN Prefer DW on Google Hungarian Prime Minister Peter Magyar (left, pictured here with Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelenskyy) said his visit to Ukraine marked the beginning of a new chapter in the relationship between Kyiv and Budapest Image: Genya Savilov/AFP Advertisement The location and the gesture were carefully chosen: Hungarian Prime Minister Peter Magyar and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy stood side by side, laid flowers and bowed their heads at the military cemetery in the center of the Ukrainian city of Uzhhorod. One of those buried there is an ethnic Hungarian who was one of the first soldiers killed in Russia's full-scale war of aggression against Ukraine . Magyar intentionally chose not to begin his first visit to Ukraine as prime minister at a government building. Instead, his Tuesday afternoon visit began at a place where he could demonstrate his solidarity with Ukraine more clearly than anywhere else. Uzhhorod, known as Ungvar in Hungarian, is the capital of Ukraine's Transcarpathia region, which is home to around 80,000 members of Ukraine's Hungarian minority. Thousands of ethnic Hungarians are fighting Russian occupying forces on the front lines. For Hungary , where ethnic Hungarian minorities in neighboring countries traditionally play an important role, the war is therefore closer to home than it is for other European countries. Magyar described his visit to Ukraine as a "historic day" in a Facebook post. Before the ceremony at the cemetery in Uzhhorod, he said: "I bring with me the solidarity of the Hungarian people. We stand with Ukraine against the Russian aggressor." Zelenskyy responded on X, saying "We appreciate this gesture of respect toward those who sacrificed their lives for Ukraine's independence." From low point to fresh start The meeting between Magyar and Zelenskyy marked a turning point in Hungary's approach to Ukraine. The two leaders repeatedly shook hands throughout the day. Such scenes would have been unthinkable just a few months ago. The propaganda of Magyar's pro-Russian predecessor, Viktor Orban , portrayed Ukraine as a "mafia state" and "lawless country" on an almost daily basis. Under Orban, relations between Hungary and Ukraine reached a historic low . Now the two countries are seeking a political reset, which is important not only for Hungary and Ukraine but for Europe as a whole. After all, Orban's repeated obstruction of support for Ukraine drove the EU to the brink of despair. Closer economic cooperation During talks in Uzhhorod, the two leaders also agreed to closer economic cooperation. Hungary's Prime Minister Peter Magyar (left) and Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelenskyy laid wreaths and flowers at a ceremony commemorating the Ukrainian defenders who fell during the Russian invasion Image: Janos Nemes/MTI/AP Photo/picture alliance The talks centered on Hungarian diesel supplies to Ukraine, greater use of Ukrainian gas storage facilities by Hungarian companies, and joint infrastructure projects, including the opening of new border crossings and a direct rail link between Budapest and Kyiv. Nevertheless, no formal agreements were signed on Tuesday. At a subsequent news conference, journalists asked questions about sensitive issues between the two countries: minority rights, Ukraine's EU integration and a new EU loan for Ukraine. Throughout the day, the two men were visibly keen to avoid any discord. Magyar, for example, described his angry outburst over Ukraine's "Carpathian Eight" initiative in parliament in late September as a "misunderstanding" and suggested that Hungary might, after all, take part. Zelenskyy's cautious replies to journalists suggest that he knows his country's path to EU membership also runs through Budapest. A fresh — but not always smooth — start One of Magyar's statements on Tuesday was key: "We've finally put a stop to this completely unnecessary and inexplicable political escalation." Even before taking office in early May 2026, Magyar had promised to reset relations with Ukraine. But the process has not been entirely smooth. Posters belonging to Viktor Orban's Fidesz party portrayed Volodymyr Zelenskyy, Peter Magyar and Ursula von der Leyen as a risk and Fidesz as 'the better choice' in the run-up to the parliamentary election in April Image: Martin Fejer/estost.net/EST&OST/IMAGO In many respects — but certainly not all — Magyar is distancing himself from his predecessor. He has made no bones of the fact that he sees Russia as the aggressor, but he rejects both arms deliveries to Ukraine and even the transit of weapons across Hungarian territory. Magyar previously accused Ukraine of treating ethnic Hungarians as second-class citizens — a claim that is not borne out by the facts. He pressed for greater minority rights and for a time blocked the opening of negotiating chapters in Ukraine's EU accession talks. Magyar also departed from diplomatic convention by choosing the location of his meeting with Zelenskyy in Ukraine: Indeed, it was Magyar who invited Zelenskyy to Transcarpathia. Hungarian attitudes to Ukraine Magyar's sometimes confrontational tone toward Ukraine can also be explained by the need to avoid appearing too pro-Ukrainian to the Hungarian public. According to a November 2026 poll conducted by the think tank Globsec , 33% of Hungarians would now support their country providing military aid to Ukraine. Although this is much more than during Orban's time in office, many Hungarians remain skeptical of Ukraine. That's why Olena Halushka, a Ukrainian political scientist at the International Centre for Ukrainian Victory (ICUV), sees some aspects of Magyar's visit as a concession to public opinion in Hungary. A monument to members of the military killed during Russia's war in Ukraine in the city of Berehove, the political and cultural center of Ukraine's Hungarian minority Image: Hanna Sokolova-Stekh/DW "Magyar has taken over a deeply polarized country," she told DW's Ukrainian Service. "A visit to Transcarpathia is more of a step for the Hungarian population than for Ukraine." Ukraine accommodated not only Magyar's choice of location but also Hungary's demands for better protection of minority rights, which were set out in a 10-point plan in June. That's because EU integration is one of the country's top political priorities. After planned restrictions on the use of minority languages were withdrawn in late 2023, Ukraine's parliament in early October passed a law on minority language rights that in some respects goes even further than European standards. Hungary subsequently dropped its obstruction of the opening of negotiating clusters for Ukraine's EU accession. 'Historic' meeting Laszlo Zubanics, chairman of the Hungarian Democratic Federation in Ukraine (UMDSZ, one of two Hungarian political parties in Transcarpathia), told DW that the Magyar-Zelenskyy meeting was "historic." He particularly welcomed the fact that Ukraine will probably implement practical improvements in the protection of minority rights "not only by the end of 2027, but much sooner, within just a few months." Laszlo Zubanics welcomed the fact that Ukraine is likely to implement practical improvements in the protection of minority rights 'within just a few months' Image: Hanna Sokolova-Stekh/DW A Hungarian diplomat who spoke to DW on condition of anonymity also called the meeting "historic," adding that after the Orban government's anti-Ukrainian policies, trust now needs to be rebuilt, and that personal meetings between the two leaders play an important role in that process. The diplomat went on to say that Hungary not only wants to ensure that the rights of the Hungarian minority are protected, it also has a strong interest in being involved in Ukraine's reconstruction. Overall, the diplomat concluded, both sides are very keen to expand economic cooperation. A path forward Hungarian political scientist Daniel Hegedus of the Institute for European Politics ( IEP ) in Berlin told DW that while the meeting was a "symbolic milestone," it will be important to see "how the two political leaders capitalize on the symbolic political capital generated by this meeting." No observers have suggested that this is the grand finale of reconciliation between Hungary and Ukraine. Nevertheless, Tuesday's reset sends an important signal to Europe, namely that if the political will is there, a deep gulf that has existed for years can be transformed into a set of diverging interests that can be addressed through negotiations. Or, as Zelenskyy put it, now there are "all the opportunities to build hopefully constructive relations." This article was originally published in German.
